name: HTTP Versions
intent: Understand how HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 move many resources over the network, and why each version was invented to remove the previous one's bottleneck.
scenario: A web page needs 60 small files: scripts, styles, images and API calls. How fast it loads depends less on the size of the files than on how many round trips the protocol needs to fetch them all.
problem: A page is dozens of requests. If each request waits for the previous response, or each needs its own connection with its own handshake, the page spends most of its time waiting for the network rather than transferring data. And one lost packet can stall unrelated downloads that share a connection.

howItWorks.title: HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection
howItWorks.text: A connection carries one request and response at a time. Keep-alive reuses the connection, but requests still queue behind each other. Browsers work around this by opening about six connections per host, each with its own TCP and TLS setup, and developers bundled files and spread them over domains to go faster.

howItWorks.title: HTTP/2: many streams over one connection
howItWorks.text: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests as interleaved streams over a single connection, compresses repeated headers, and allows prioritisation. One connection and one handshake replace six. The bundling tricks are no longer needed.

howItWorks.title: HTTP/2's remaining problem: TCP head-of-line blocking
howItWorks.text: All streams share one TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes in order. When a single packet is lost, every stream behind it waits for the retransmission, even streams whose data already arrived. On lossy mobile networks this can make HTTP/2 slower than several HTTP/1.1 connections.

howItWorks.title: HTTP/3: the same ideas over QUIC
howItWorks.text: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport built on UDP. QUIC implements reliability per stream, so a lost packet only delays the stream it belongs to. It also combines the transport and TLS handshakes into one round trip, can resume with zero round trips, and survives a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data because connections are identified by an id, not by the IP address.

howItWorks.title: Negotiation and fallback
howItWorks.text: Clients and servers agree on a version during the connection (ALPN for HTTP/2, and an Alt-Svc hint for HTTP/3). If UDP is blocked, the client falls back to HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1. Servers and CDNs usually support all three, so enabling the newer versions is mostly configuration.

pros: HTTP/2: fewer connections, multiplexing and header compression make pages faster with no code changes
HTTP/3: no TCP head-of-line blocking, faster setup, resilient to network changes
Automatic negotiation and fallback keep old clients working
CDNs and modern servers support them out of the box
cons: HTTP/2 still suffers when a single lossy TCP connection stalls everything
HTTP/3 needs UDP to get through, and uses more CPU on servers
Older optimisations (domain sharding, giant bundles) can hurt on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
Debugging encrypted, multiplexed protocols needs better tools
whenToUse: Enable HTTP/2 everywhere, and HTTP/3 where your CDN or server supports it
Mobile and high-latency audiences benefit most from HTTP/3
Serve many small resources and let multiplexing handle them
whenNotToUse: Keep HTTP/1.1 fallback available for old clients and strict networks
Do not rely on a protocol upgrade to fix pages that fetch far too much data
pitfalls: Domain sharding and image sprites kept from the HTTP/1.1 era
Assuming HTTP/2 always beats HTTP/1.1 on poor networks
Blocking UDP at the firewall and wondering why HTTP/3 is never used
Judging protocols on a fast office network instead of real, lossy mobile ones
